understanding.insight: It is not that you do not know what you are doing. It is that the years of trying without a win have taught you to blame yourself for something the years themselves did.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section praising learning: the three kinds of people.
verse.sanskrit: प्रारभ्यते न खलु विघ्नभयेन नीचैः प्रारभ्य विघ्नविहता विरमन्ति मध्याः ॥ विघ्नैः पुनः पुनरपि प्रतिहन्यमानाः प्रारब्धमुत्तमगुणा न परित्यजन्ति ॥
verse.line: Some never start for fear of obstacles; some quit when obstacles hit. The best keep going.
verse.translation: The lowest do not begin at all, for fear of obstacles. The middling begin, but stop when obstacles strike. The best, struck by obstacles again and again, do not give up what they have begun.
verse.why: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.
verse.misuse: Perseverance is not refusing ever to change course; weigh honestly whether the goal still deserves you.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: In praise of learning and the learned
prasang.summary: Bhartrihari praises learning as wealth no thief can take and speech as the one lasting ornament, then turns to good company and the three kinds of people who face obstacles. It ends with the 'sword's-edge vow' of the good.
prasang.lesson: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari is describing the three kinds of people who face obstacles. Some never begin, afraid of what might go wrong. Some begin, but stop the moment a problem appears. The best, however, are struck again and again, and still they do not let go of what they started.
verse.for_you: You have been building apps for years and the result is nothing. You do not know if you are disciplined or stubborn. This verse names that stuckness. It says some quit when obstacles hit, but the best keep going.

verse.speaker: A brahmin (retold by Bhishma)
verse.setting: The brahmin's counsel to King Senajit, contrasting comfort and capable effort.
verse.sanskrit: सुखं दुःखान्तमालस्यं दुःखं दाक्ष्यं सुखोदयम् / भूतिश्चैव श्रिया सार्धं दक्षे वसति नालसे
verse.line: Idleness feels good and ends in misery. Effort feels hard and ends in happiness.
verse.translation: Idleness feels pleasant but ends in sorrow; capable effort feels hard but gives rise to happiness. Good fortune and prosperity live with the capable, not with the idle.
verse.why: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.
verse.misuse: Effort is not overwork; rest is not idleness.

prasang.title: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasang.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

verse.meaning: A brahmin speaks to King Senajit, who is crushed by grief, and says that idleness feels good but ends in misery, while capable effort feels hard but gives rise to happiness. Good fortune lives with the capable, not with the idle.
verse.for_you: The years of building your apps have felt hard and unrewarded, and you are tired of the doubt. But the pattern beneath this is not failure. It is the cycle of delay that has run its course. You are not the one who stopped knowing what to do.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वतो नार्थसिद्धिर्मे भवतीति ह भारत / निर्वेदो नात्र गन्तव्यो द्वावन्तौ यस्य कर्मणः
verse.line: Don't despair because effort hasn't paid off yet. Every attempt can go either way.
verse.translation: 'I keep working and still don't succeed' is no reason to despair. Every effort can end two ways, in success or not; only by not acting is the outcome certain.
verse.why: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

prasang.title: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

verse.meaning: Draupadi tells Yudhishthira not to despair because effort has not paid off. Every attempt can end two ways, in success or not. Only by not acting is the outcome certain. She argues that waiting on fate is no plan, and people must act.
verse.for_you: You are holding onto the work even when the results have not come. The effort is not lost. The day does not have to be measured by a win. You can hold that the work itself is the thing to keep, and let the outcome wait.

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: निश्चित्य यः प्रक्रमते नान्तर्वसति कर्मणः / अवन्ध्यकालो वश्यात्मा स वै पण्डित उच्यते
verse.line: Decide, then begin. Don't stall halfway, don't waste time, and keep yourself steady.
verse.translation: One who begins only after deciding, does not stop halfway through the work, does not waste time and keeps himself in hand, is called wise.
verse.why: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

prasang.lesson: Decide calmly, act steadily, forgive freely, and know what real happiness is made of.

verse.for_you: You have been building these apps for years while carrying work and family. The effort is not lost. Today, let the work itself be enough. Keep your hands steady on the task. The day does not have to end with a win.

verse.speaker: Sanatkumara
verse.setting: A step in Sanatkumara's ladder: faith rests on steadiness, steadiness on action.
verse.sanskrit: यदा वै करोत्यथ निस्तिष्ठति नाकृत्वा निस्तिष्ठति कृत्वैव निस्तिष्ठति कृतिस्त्वेव विजिज्ञासितव्येति कृतिं भगवो विजिज्ञास इति ॥
verse.line: Steadiness comes from doing. No one becomes steady without acting; act, and steadiness follows.
verse.translation: When one acts, one becomes steadfast. One does not become steadfast without acting; only by acting does one become steadfast. So action itself must be understood. 'Sir, I wish to understand action.'
verse.why: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

prasang.title: Narada: learned but sad
prasang.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.
prasang.story_hook: Narada knew every subject worth knowing, and still came to Sanatkumara feeling sad.
prasang.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

verse.meaning: Narada comes to Sanatkumara, learned in every science but deeply unhappy. Sanatkumara leads him up a ladder from names to action, and then to joy, and finally to the infinite. He says that when one acts, one becomes steadfast, and one does not become steadfast without acting. Action itself must be understood.
verse.for_you: But steadiness comes from doing. Pick one small, visible thing about the app today, and do it before you feel ready. Let the action come first, and let the steadiness follow.

verse.speaker: Hanuman
verse.setting: Having searched all of Lanka without finding Sita, Hanuman fights off despair.
verse.sanskrit: अनिर्वेदः श्रियो मूलमनिर्वेदः परं सुखम्। भूयस्तत्र विचेष्यामि न यत्र विचयः कृतः॥
verse.line: Refusing to lose heart is the root of success. Look again where you have not yet looked.
verse.translation: Not losing heart is the root of success; not losing heart is the highest happiness. I will search again, in the places I have not yet searched.
verse.why: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

prasang.title: Hanuman's search and near despair
prasang.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
prasang.story_hook: Hanuman had searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and she was nowhere.
prasang.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

verse.meaning: Hanuman stands in Lanka, having searched all night without finding Sita. Despair is close, the cost of failure heavy, but he tells himself to refuse losing heart. He says he will search again, in the places he has not yet looked. The verse proposes that when you have looked everywhere, the next step is simply to look again. Steadiness does not come first. It comes from doing, from acting again in the very place you have already tried.
verse.for_you: You have looked at your apps, your code, your plan, and found nothing. Today, look again where you have not yet looked. Open the project folder, not to fix it, but to see one file you have not opened in months. That is the small act that starts.

story.summary: Ram waits three days for the ocean to let him pass, then loses patience. The ocean reveals that Nala can build a bridge; Nala admits his skill and the whole army hauls trees and rocks for five days until the bridge reaches Lanka.
story.lesson: Big things get built by many hands, once someone admits they know how.

script: You are carrying years of side projects that have gone nowhere. You have a job, children, and aging parents to look after. You keep building apps because stopping feels like admitting defeat. But the real exhaustion is not the work. It is the feeling that you do not know what is wrong with you.
Bhartrihari sits down to write the Niti Shatakam. He is thinking about the different ways people face difficulty. He describes three types of people. The lowest never start at all. Bhartrihari said:
प्रारभ्यते न खलु विघ्नभयेन नीचैः प्रारभ्य विघ्नविहता विरमन्ति मध्याः. विघ्नैः पुनः पुनरपि प्रतिहन्यमानाः प्रारब्धमुत्तमगुणा न परित्यजन्ति.
In plain words: Some never start for fear of obstacles; some quit when obstacles hit. The best keep going.

This is about how people handle the moment things get hard. It is easy to blame yourself when you feel stuck. But the text is not saying you are failing by trying. It is saying something else is at work. The years without a win have taught you to doubt every step. The problem is not that you are stubborn. The problem is that you have forgotten how to begin again. This is easier said than done, because the mind has made staying stuck feel like the only safe choice.

Look at the last app you started. It did not fail because you are not good enough. It stopped because the first push felt too heavy. Today, do not try to finish the whole thing. Just open the workspace. Let the code sit there for ten minutes. That is the only push you need today.
What is the smallest part of your work that you can touch today?

depth.life: You are in the middle of the day, between your job and the next thing, and you are wondering if the years of building apps are discipline or just stubbornness. You keep going, but you do not know if you are stuck or if you are just slow.
depth.points: The obstacle is not a single failure. It is the long stretch where you keep trying without a win, and the mind starts to think the effort itself is the problem.
depth.practice: Pick one tiny part of the app and work on it for ten minutes. No big goal, just a small step forward.
depth.question: What would it mean to call this persistence instead of stubbornness?
